hints: For any probability density function the total area under the curve is 1, so $\int \text{f}(x)\,\text{d}x = 1$. The density is only non-zero from 0 to 1, so those are your limits: $k\int_0^1 (x - x^2)\,\text{d}x = 1$.
Integrate $x - x^2$ term by term with the power rule: raise the power by 1 and divide by the new power. Keep $k$ as a constant factor outside.
Substitute the limits 1 and 0 into your integral, combine the fractions $\dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\dfrac{1}{3}$ and set the result equal to 1, then solve for $k$ so that you end exactly on 6.
walkthrough:
**Why the area must equal 1**

$\text{f}$ is a probability density function. The total probability of all possible values is 1, and the probability is the **area under the curve**. So the whole area under the graph must be 1.

The curve (see the diagram) is only above the axis between $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, and is zero elsewhere. So we only integrate from 0 to 1:

$$\int_0^1 k(x - x^2)\,\text{d}x = 1$$

Writing this equation earns the **M1**.

**Integrate (first A1)**

Integrate each term: add 1 to the power and divide by the new power.

$$\int x\,\text{d}x = \frac{x^2}{2} \qquad \int x^2\,\text{d}x = \frac{x^3}{3}$$

$$k\left[\frac{x^2}{2} - \frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^1 = 1$$

This earns the first **A1**.

**Substitute the limits (second A1)**

Put in $x = 1$, then $x = 0$, and subtract (the value at 0 is zero):

$$k\left[\left(\frac{1^2}{2} - \frac{1^3}{3}\right) - \left(\frac{0^2}{2} - \frac{0^3}{3}\right)\right] = 1$$

$$k\left[\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}\right] = 1$$

Subtract the fractions with a common denominator of 6:

$$\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3} = \frac{3}{6} - \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{6}$$

$$\frac{k}{6} = 1$$

This earns the second **A1** (for a correct line with no errors seen).

**Final answer**

Multiply both sides by 6:

$$k = 6$$

which is what we were asked to show.

hints: Look at the diagram: the curve is symmetrical about the middle of the interval from 0 to 1, so the mean sits on the line of symmetry.
For the variance you need $\text{E}(X^2) = \int x^2\,\text{f}(x)\,\text{d}x$ over 0 to 1. Use $k = 6$ and multiply out $x^2(x - x^2)$ before integrating.
Use $\text{Var}(X) = \text{E}(X^2) - \left[\text{E}(X)\right]^2$, with your mean from the first hint.
Integrate $6(x^3 - x^4)$, substitute the limits 1 and 0, then subtract the square of the mean. A variance can never be negative, so check your final sign.
walkthrough:
**The mean from the symmetry (B1)**

The curve in the diagram is a symmetrical arch between $x = 0$ and $x = 1$ (indeed $x - x^2 = x(1-x)$ is symmetrical about the middle). For a symmetrical distribution the mean is at the centre of symmetry:

$$\text{E}(X) = \frac{0 + 1}{2} = 0.5$$

This earns the **B1**. (You could also check by integrating $6\int_0^1 x(x - x^2)\,\text{d}x = 6\left[\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4}\right] = 0.5$.)

**Set up E(X²) (first M1)**

The variance formula is $\text{Var}(X) = \text{E}(X^2) - [\text{E}(X)]^2$. For a continuous variable

$$\text{E}(X^2) = \int x^2\,\text{f}(x)\,\text{d}x = 6\int_0^1 x^2(x - x^2)\,\text{d}x$$

Multiply out the bracket: $x^2 \times x = x^3$ and $x^2 \times x^2 = x^4$.

$$\text{E}(X^2) = 6\int_0^1 (x^3 - x^4)\,\text{d}x$$

This earns the first **M1**.

**Integrate and evaluate E(X²)**

$$\text{E}(X^2) = 6\left[\frac{x^4}{4} - \frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^1$$

At $x = 1$: $\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{5} = \frac{5}{20} - \frac{4}{20} = \frac{1}{20}$. At $x = 0$ the value is 0.

$$\text{E}(X^2) = 6 \times \frac{1}{20} = 0.3$$

**Subtract the mean squared (second M1)**

$$\text{Var}(X) = \text{E}(X^2) - [\text{E}(X)]^2 = 0.3 - 0.5^2$$

$$0.5^2 = 0.25$$

$$0.3 - 0.25 = 0.05$$

This line earns the second **M1** (the result must be positive; a negative variance means a mistake).

hints: $\text{f}(x) = 0$ for $x > 1$, so no probability lies between 1 and 2. The probability is the area under $6(x - x^2)$, and only the part from 0.4 up to 1 contributes.
Substitute the limits into the integral from part (i), $6\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]$: put in the upper limit, subtract the value at the lower limit, $0.4$.
Work out $\dfrac{0.4^2}{2} - \dfrac{0.4^3}{3}$ carefully and the bracket $\dfrac{1}{2} - \dfrac{1}{3}$, then subtract and multiply by 6.
walkthrough:
**Why the upper limit is 1, not 2 (M1)**

$\text{P}(0.4 < X < 2)$ is the area under the curve between $x = 0.4$ and $x = 2$. But $\text{f}(x) = 0$ for every $x$ above 1, so there is no area between 1 and 2. The area is the same as $\text{P}(0.4 < X < 1)$:

$$\text{P}(0.4 < X < 2) = 6\int_{0.4}^{1}(x - x^2)\,\text{d}x$$

This earns the **M1**. (The scheme also gives the M1 if you keep 2 as the upper limit.)

**Substitute the limits (A1 FT)**

Use $\left[\dfrac{x^2}{2} - \dfrac{x^3}{3}\right]$ from part (i), putting in the upper limit and subtracting the lower limit:

$$6\left\{\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{3}\right) - \left(\frac{0.4^2}{2} - \frac{0.4^3}{3}\right)\right\}$$

This earns the **A1 FT**.
